svg.aria-label: Diagram: the limits that bound a Privileged Access Manager entitlement, why temporary access is implemented as timed allow-policy bindings and therefore inherits access change propagation and conflicts with authoritative Terraform, which roles cannot be placed behind just-in-time elevation, and which approval controls are still Preview and licence-gated
svg.title: Privileged Access Manager: real just-in-time elevation, built from timed allow-policy bindings
svg.text: Elevation that genuinely expires — and is still an allow-policy binding underneath.
Which means it starts and ends on the propagation clock, and makes PAM another writer to your policy.
An entitlement, and the numbers that bound it
Maximum grant duration
7 days — range 1800s to 604800s
Roles per entitlement
up to 30
Requesting principals
up to 20, or more via a group
Open grants per user, per entitlement
Approval deadline, immediate activation
24 hours, then Expired
Grants are deleted 30 days after they are denied, revoked, withdrawn, expired, or ended.
It is allow-policy bindings underneath, which has two consequences
PAM manages temporary access by adding and removing role bindings, with time-based IAM Conditions.
So activation AND revocation depend on standard access change propagation, the #52 numbers.
And PAM is now another writer to your allow policy. Authoritative Terraform will fight it:
the docs say use NON-AUTHORITATIVE resources so Terraform does not override PAM bindings.
What you cannot put behind just-in-time
PAM does not support the legacy basic roles: Owner, Editor and Viewer.
So the broadest standing grants in most estates are exactly the ones it cannot temporalise.
It also only covers services that support granular access through IAM.
The controls you would most want are Preview, and licence-gated
Multi-party and multi-level approval: PREVIEW, and needs Security Command Center Enterprise
or Premium tier. Up to 2 sequential levels, up to 5 approvers per level.
Also Preview: scope customisation, grant scheduling, withdrawal, service-account approvers.
GA today is the single-approver path, plus you cannot approve your own request.
Service accounts and agent identities can be APPROVERS, and can self-elevate. Useful for
pipelines, and worth deciding deliberately: an automated approver is not a second person.
#53 conditions that fail open. #54 elevation that is real, bounded and audited, and is still
an allow-policy binding, so it starts and ends on the propagation clock, not on the button.
